_note: R1 prose blocks: 3-6 sentences of mathematical characterization (what the object is, boundary behaviour), matching what the reasoning scaffold requests. R0 cells use (dossier -> signature -> definition); R1 cells use (dossier -> signature -> prose -> definition) over the SAME three definitions.
Fin.contractNth: The object is a reindexing operator on finite tuples: given a tuple of length n+1 and a binary operation, it produces a tuple of length n by collapsing two adjacent entries into one. The index j names the collapse point, and the three regions of the output are determined by position relative to j: entries strictly before j are copied unchanged, the entry at j is the operation applied to the two original entries straddling that position, and entries after j are copied from the shifted original. The boundary behaviour is entirely in the middle case — it is the only index at which the operation is applied at all, and it consumes two source entries rather than one, which is why the output is one shorter than the input. Because the domain and codomain have different lengths, the two copying branches must use different index coercions: the earlier region embeds an index of the shorter tuple into the longer one, while the later region steps past the collapsed pair.
Nat.ceilRoot: The object is the n-th root of a natural number rounded upward in the divisibility order: it acts on the prime factorization by dividing every exponent by n and rounding each quotient up. Concretely, if a factors as a product of prime powers, the result is the product of those same primes raised to the ceilings of their exponents divided by n. The boundary conventions are both degenerate cases collapsing to a single value: when n is zero there is no meaningful root to take, and when a is zero it has no factorization to act on, so both return zero. The rounding direction is the whole content of the definition — rounding down instead gives a different and equally natural operation, so the choice must be explicit rather than implied. In order-theoretic terms this is the left adjoint of raising to the n-th power, which is exactly what rounding up rather than down secures.
SimpleGraph.LocallyLinear: The object is a property of a simple graph asserting that its triangles cover its edges exactly once. It decomposes into two independent requirements that together give the 'exactly one' reading: no two distinct triangles may share an edge, and every edge must lie in at least one triangle. Neither half suffices alone — a graph with no triangles at all satisfies the disjointness clause vacuously, while a graph whose triangles overlap satisfies the covering clause but not uniqueness. The property is stated over all edges of the graph, so it is a universally quantified condition guarded by adjacency, with the covering half supplying an existential witness for each edge.
Set.InjOn: The object is injectivity restricted to a subset rather than asserted of a whole function: the function may collide freely outside the set, and nothing is claimed about such collisions. The condition ranges over pairs of points, and each point is guarded by membership in the set before the equality hypothesis is used, so the implication only ever fires for pairs drawn from the set. When the set is empty the property holds vacuously, and when the set is everything it coincides with ordinary injectivity. The two membership guards are hypotheses of the implication rather than conditions on the conclusion, which is what makes the property behave correctly under passing to subsets.
Filter.limsSup: The object is the limit superior of a filter, defined not by a construction but by a characterization: it is the least element that eventually dominates. Precisely, consider the collection of all elements that the filter eventually stays below, and take the infimum of that collection. Nothing is computed here — the definition names the object by the property that distinguishes it, and existence rests on the ambient order being sufficiently complete for the infimum to exist. The boundary behaviour follows from that same completeness: when no element eventually dominates, the collection is empty and the infimum is the top of the order; when every element does, it is the bottom. This shape — the least (or greatest) element satisfying an eventual or universal condition — is the honest form for many objects that admit no algorithm.
SuccChain: The object is a one-step successor operation on chains of a relation: given a set, it returns a strictly larger chain when one exists, and otherwise returns the set unchanged. The definition is a characterization rather than a construction, because when several strictly larger chains exist the definition commits to no particular one — it selects a witness, and any witness will do for the purposes the object serves. The boundary case is the whole reason the definition is total: when the set admits no strict chain extension, there is nothing to select, and returning the set unchanged makes the operation defined everywhere. This fixed-point behaviour at the boundary is what allows the operation to be iterated without a separate termination condition.
